body: When the array values change from {1,12,3,-4,2} to {-4,6,1,0,-1}, the return values for count should be 4 and i should be 0. Why? Well num is still 7, and none of the numbers in the array are larger than 7. Thus, we loop or iterate through the array in its entirety. starting from -1 which is array[4] to -4 which is array[0]. None of the values are large enough to meet the first if statement:      if (array[i] > num){            return i;     }  None of the values in the array are large enough to fulfill this requirement. Thus, nothing is returned from that if statement. It is not until we get to the final return statement that we are able to return a value. That is when we iterate through the while loop and are at the end of the array.

title: Catch division by zero
body: Hi all, it seems to me the assignment leads to confusion: "[...] It should be possible to input an array with 0 elements, the program should handle it and it should not throw an exception." Given the previous exercises I assume they mean that the program must be able to handle arrays with elements of value 0. The way it is currently stated however, the assignment is to have it handle empty arrays, which in fact it already does.  So assuming we have to handle elements with value 0, we need to introduce a check on the value of array[k] before calculating the division:              if (array[k]!=0) {                 arrayResults[k] = number/array[k];             }  On top of that we can add a check when printing the results to see if the input value (arr[i]) is zero. If so, the value printed should not be 0.0, but something that tells the user it was a division by zero.          for (int i=0; i< arrResult.length;i++) { 	        System.out.println("array[" + i +"] = " +  	            ((arr[i] != 0) ? arrResult[i] : "DIV(0)")); 	    }  Read as "If arr[i] is not equal to zero then print arrResult[i], else print DIV(0)."  Complete code:      public class Main {         static double[] divisions(int number, int[] array){	             double [] arrayResults = new double[array.length];             for (int k = 0; k < array.length; k++) {                 if (array[k]!=0) {                     arrayResults[k] = number/array[k];                 }             }             return arrayResults;         }              public static void main(String[] args) {             int [] arr = {5, 12, 0 , 1};                     double[] arrResult= divisions(154, arr);     	    	     for (int i=0; i< arrResult.length;i++){ 	            System.out.println("array[" + i +"] = " +  	                ((arr[i] != 0) ? arrResult[i] : "DIV(0)")); 	        }         }     }

title: The problem is the For-loop
body: The for-loop only takes into account the values in the first array (route1). It also iterates through the 2 other arrays, but only up to the length of the first array (route1):      for(int i = 0; i < **route1.length**; i++)  This means that there are values in the 2 other arrays that are not added to the sum sum2 and sum3 respectively. Namely the values in these arrays that are in positions higher than the length of the first array.  One should make 2 other for-loops so that there is one for-loop for each array:      for(int i = 0; i < route1.length; i++)             {                 sum1 += route1[i];             }             for(int i = 0; i < route2.length; i++)             {                 sum2 += route2[i];             }             for(int i = 0; i < route3.length; i++)             {                 sum3 += route3[i];             }

body: You are right in that !a is the same as !a&&b in this case. However the power of assertions lies partly in that they also serve as documentation. In this particular branch, we expect that a will be false and b will be true, so that this is a good way to write the assertion. If we had made a mistake, such as writing !!b in the previous branch, the assertion would pick this up. It is a matter of taste, of course, but writing !a&&b is definitely not a mistake.

body: Dear students:  Each program o method can have a different specification. In this case, we have a different method (sqrt(int)) to calculate the square root that uses the Java API (Math.sqrt()). So, in some cases, it could be considered that sqrt(0) is a valid argument, but it is not this example. Even, sqrt(0) would not be calculated, simply the argument is returned as specified in the API. We could include all "special cases" included in the API, but it is not our goal.   So, in the method definition has been clarified that the argument is an "integer number" greater than 0, therefore, values between 0 and 1 cannot be used as argument; therefore, this last case would be not a postcondition.  Many thanks and regards,  Florina

Factorial, like Fibonnaci increases really fast i.e. (15!) = 2004310016 which is getting pretty close to how much "int" type of the variable can handle which causes a StackOverFlow.   At (17!) is already over the limit range of an int which is 2,147,483,647(inclusive).  That is what I think but I could be wrong. A quick fix would be to use a long type but won't help you on the long run. The other way would be to make use of an iterative algorithm or using Big Integer object. That should keep it going for a while. Have a look [here][1],  or [here][2] and [here][3]  I've provided some references. body: Dear Sarma,  maybe it is due to the existence of other processes (programs in execution) executing at the same time in codeboard or in your PC.   This is one of the main problems that we face if we want to measure execution time. In order to the measure to be really accurate, there should be only the minimal amount of processes into the machine (it is not the intention of this exercise, the main aim of the exercise is to give you a clue about the order of magnitude of the execution time).  Internally, your computer uses 1,2 or 4 CPUs. However,to explain it better I will simplify it to only 1 CPU (and we will imagine that each Java thread is mapped into a process, it is not always like this) (this explanation is an over simplification of what really is happening at CPU level).   Usually, the CPU time used by the different processes is divided in slots or slices. One process goes into the CPU for the first time, executes a number of sentences, finishes its "slot", stores all its info into a table of processes and goes to the queue again to wait to be selected by the scheduling algorithm.   Depending on the scheduling algorithm used, the next process to execute could be the one that is waiting more, the one with the closer deadline, the one with more priority, the one with a greater period, there are a lot of scheduling algorithms... For example, Linux uses Completely Fair Scheduling https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completely_Fair_Scheduler If you are interested in this, check here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduling_(computing)#Summary  If you finish the for loop before going again to the process queue, then the time that we are measuring is the "real" execution time. However, if your slot finishes before and other process  goes into the CPU, you should wait until it finishes its slice and you can finish your loop (and the execution time increases). title: JavaDoc precondition postcondition recommendation
category_name: Week 2 / Preconditions and Postconditions: FuelTank (non graded activity)
body:
For any that are struggling with the javadoc comments for pre and post conditions here are my recommendations based upon observation: I recommend the following format: /** * Add fuel to the tank * *
*
precondition : amount > 0.0 *
precondition : amount<=getTankMax()-getTankLevel() *
postcondition : not empty() *
* * @param amount the amount of fuel to add * */ My reasoning: 1. **Use lower case for pre and post condition.** If we did have the plugin to make use of @precondition and @postcondition, both words would be lower case. 2. **Locate the precondition and postcondition statements in between the description and the @ tags.** If we place these statements before the description it would separate the @precondition @param block tags and also look different than many of the current conventions where the description is always first. If we place these statements after the @param @return block tags they will be indented and “included” in the last block tag section that was defined prior to the precondition and postcondition statements. 3. **Use `
` and `
` tags to separate the content from the rest.** By making use of HTML markup we follow along with best practice for making javadocs readable. By only using simple markup in the front of these statements, it allows us to view the content in code form as well as javadoc form with ease. 4. **Only use `
`, `
` tags in front.** If we write a conversion program, we can use simple regular expressions to parse out the `
` and `
` tags and convert them into @ symbols, creating new block tags for when we install the javadoc plugin. `/\*
/g`
`/\*
/g` 5. **@param and @return are both are position independent.** Therefore placing the @precondition before the @param statements should not cause any issues when generating javadocs, if the plugins were created well.

body: You are right: We can only conclude from the given description that n should be the array length - 1.    Otherwise, the method doesn't sort the entire array or leads to an index out of bound error. It would be clearer if this was mentioned explicitly.  The algorithm presented shows the so called bubble sort. It consists of two nested loops. On each iteration of the outer loop (the for loop), numbers are "bubbled" to the right in the inner loop (the while loop) - if they are smaller than the following number, else they stay where they are.      One single iteration of the outer loop will not sort the array - but if you repeat the procedure until all numbers are "bubbled" into the right place, the array will finally be sorted.  There's a nice video on youtube showing a [danced bubblesort][1]  from a hungarian folk dance group (they have also videos of other sorting algorithms....) body: Dear Shella5 and bribre,  as bribre said, the point of this first quarter is to make you aware of the problematic of using empirical tests to measure the execution time of which algorithm is best from a set of different implementations. It is used as  motivation for the concepts explained later in the week.  When you are trying to measure seriously the execution time of an algorithm (for example to run it on a real-time system where human lifes can be threatened if it does not meet a deadline), you should run it a lot of times and usually over an almost "naked" machine, that is, no windows system (in linux no X11), no unnecessary service daemons (such as printer and so on), only the kernel in linux and that's all. And even in this conditions, if possible, it is better to perform some static or hybrid WCET (worst case execution time) analysis technique (certification authorities, such as the European Aviation Safety Agency, rely on models to analyse the WCET in order to certificate a software with real-time requirements). It is a whole field of research here (and very important).   If you want to know more about this:  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worst-case_execution_time  Moreover, there are commercial applications that allow you to perform a profile (memory used, execution time, etc), of your code. We have here the same problem, usually, they are profiling the paths that they are exploring with certain input parameters... Many times it is impossible to check all the possible inputs for a certain algorithm (only think on a simple algorithm that accept an integer, you cannot check all the possible inputs, as they are infinite).   But the point of the exercise was to give you an idea of the order of magnitude, not to evaluate seriously their performance.  bribre, the thread that you are talking about is:  https://courses.edx.org/courses/course-v1:UC3Mx+IT.1.2x+2016T2/discussion/forum/f815787b3379840fbfff5bd8fb497fdf4c289e5d/threads/57332da2d11155057e000ac8  Thank yo

If n-1 elements are in place, the last one must be on its right place, too.  To sort the array, the for loop only needs to run length-of-array - 1 times.       Though, the condition of the while loop requires that n is equal to the length of the array: The maximum value for k must be length-of-array - 1.   Thank you for pointing out this issue!   To avoid the unnecessary iteration, I would change the condition of the while loop to   `(while (k != n+1))`   and choose n equal to length-of-array - 1

body: So the more I look at the code, the more I would have chosen to use a different name for the validation of the tank being empty.  When we create names for our methods and classes they should follow closely to what is actually being done.  For example if I state in black box testing:  >     FuelTank tank = new FuelTank(40,10); >     System.out.println("Running FuelTank.empty() method."); >     System.out.println("> " + tank.empty() );  It may not be clear if I am emptying the fuel tank or if I am asking if the tank is empty. Now if you carefully observed that the method returns a boolean then you might have concluded that we are using the word "empty" as an adjective in this case and it returns the state of the object.  However empty can be a verb as well. ( https://www.google.com/#q=is%20empty%20a%20verb )  And this is where language can cause a bit of havoc on our programs.  In my experience when there is ambiguity in the language it is better to error on the side of adding more descriptive text to a method name when returning object state, then to just use the word alone.  I would reserve using the word alone to represent the verb definition.  For example in our class we have `FuelTank.fill()` which actually performs the act of filling up the tank with incremental amounts.  Notice that the name implies an action.  Why not keep with this convention?  "**get**" implies a return of state for an attribute.  I would like to suggest including "**is**" in this definition to return boolean state information about our object.  So I would change   >   public boolean empty(){  to  >   public boolean isEmpty(){  and perhaps create a new function      public empty() {         tankLevel = 0;     }  we might even change FuelTank.full() to FuelTank.isFull()  Or am I missing some new thought on writing classes and why we should do otherwise?

body: Hola,  @EdwinFredy83  En la vida real, en proyectos reales, los datos pueden venir de una pantalla de entrada, y puede ser que el programa los utilice en varios métodos. Por lo tanto, es más cómodo y eficiente hacer las validaciones una sola vez, en un método o grupo de métodos concretos, y en el resto del programa ya sabes que los datos están bien. Además, para validar los datos, algunas veces tiene que acceder a una base de datos (para ver si algo existe o no). Cuanto menos accedas, más eficiente es el programa de cara al usuario, incluso de cara al sistema (aunque para eso está la cache). Suele ser mejor validar los datos al principio, y no hacer nada de nada hasta que los datos estén correctos. Porque ten en cuenta que otras veces los datos vienen en archivos de intercambio entre una empresa y otra, por ejemplo las remesas de nóminas que manda una empresa a un banco. En este caso, para el banco que recibe el archivo, lo más limpio es validar el archivo de datos, y si hay errores o incongruencias en los datos, no ejecutar nada para no tener problemas mayores en la base de datos o en los apuntes contables y cosas por el estilo. Una vez que el archivo de datos está validado y correcto, ya puedes dedicar el resto del programa, u otro programa, a procesar los datos (en casos así es un todo o nada: o se procesan todos los datos, o no se procesa ninguno, es decir, un proceso por lotes).  Personalmente, y por mi propia experiencia en el campo, siempre validar primero, y a las funciones les deben llegar siempre datos ya validados en la medida de lo posible. Un programa debe ser robusto, y hay que prever que un usuario siempre buscará (consciente o inconscientemente) romper algo. Debes darle al programa un mínimo de inteligencia para no aceptar datos incorrectos, o saber qué hacer con ellos, y/o informar al usuario, naturalmente. Como suelen decir: más vale prevenir que curar.   También es un poco como la filosofía UNIX: un programa hace sólo una cosa, pero la hace bien.

body: You only add the "throws Exception" clause if you think or suppose that an error might occur.    This means: If anything of the code you want to execute in your setup method is "risky", then you add it.     If you think the code is safe, then you don't.       Throwing an exception is a part of defensive programming: You try to forsee upcoming/potential errors. Because throwing an exception implies that the exception must be caught (otherwise the program won't compile), you ensure (up to a certain point) that your program won't crash.  For example, doing something with files is mostly "risky": The file does not exist, the path is not correct, the file is corrupted etc.     You don't want that your program crashes and handle the error (for example with amessage to the user).  You can add an exception clause to any method you write to ensure that potential errors get caught. Especially if they are used by other programmers, this is very important.     And if you use a method that throws an exception: Be sure not to forget to handle the potential error.  Concerning the setup() method that initiates a calculator: this rings the alarm bells. The first is "attention - avoid zero division error" and the second "attention - avoid integer overflow error"    Therefore, it's a good idea to add the exception clause. body: You can divide exceptions in two main groups: Checked exceptions and Unchecked exceptions.  There are two types of unchecked exceptions:    1) Errors → they usually let the program crash (e.g. stack overflow, out of memory etc.) - there's not much to be done    2) Runtime errors → they are usually due to faults introduced by the programmer (e.g. zero division, index out of bounds). It would not make sense to catch these errors, instead the code has to be corrected (and they give us a hint how to correct them)  The checked exceptions are those that are announced with the "throws" keyword in the method declaration.  This "throws XY-Exception" tells anyone who calls this method that an exception might occur and that this exception must be handled in one way or another (e.g. in a try-catch block)      Errors that fall in this category are usually not the fault of the programmer (e.g. problems with opening a file, illegal user input), but if correctly handled, the program can recover.  tl;dr:     A method that throws an exception tells the caller: Attention, an error might occur - do something to handle this error.

body: I don't know whether this course will cover the use of bitwise operations in Java.     They are generally very fast and using them wisely can improve the efficiency of our code. But treating the whole topic might go beyond the scope of this course.    Bitwise operations are a very powerful tool and it's definitively worth to dive deeper into the subject - if it's not covered by this course, you will find a lot of information and examples of using them on the Internet ;)   Concerning the example solution to the tower-of-Hanoi problem:  The binary solution represents each disk as one binary digit.    To represent n disks, you need to create a n-bit binary number, where the leftmost bit represents the largest disk and the rightmost bit the smallest.  `1 << n`      creates a (n+1)-bit number as it shifts the value 1 of the 1-bit number n places to the left and filles the vacant places with zeros.    With the loop condition     `(i = 0; i < (1 << n); i++)`    , i will take the value of the binary numbers from b(n-bits of 0) to b(n-bits of 1)  How the movement is deducted from this serie of binary numbers  is explained in this [wikipedia article][1].  The bitwise operations needed for this algorithm are bitwise AND (&) and bitwise OR (|) You might want to read the corresponding [wikipedia article][2] for the details.     [1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_Hanoi#Binary_solution   [2]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitwise_operation

body: Dear RicardoAbian,  The point of the exercise is to measure times. Never ever should you sum the times within the loop. I will explain this with an example.  Imagine that we have a machine that can only give you a precision of 10000 nanoseconds.  So, if your algorithm execution time is 5000 nanoseconds, with your code snippet, it will always say that endTime-startTime is 0. You run your loop 10000 times, and the average execution time will be 0*10000 / 10000 = 0.  However, if you measure the time before the loop run your algorithm 10000 times, and then measure again, it would say that endTime - startTime = 50000000 nanoseconds, giving you an average time of 5000 nanoseconds.  You can think on an analog clock. You usually have an accuracy of 1 second. If you want to measure your speed running (you want to know your km/h or the time that it takes you to run 1 km), you will never measure how much time it takes you to run 1 meter, you will look to your clock, memorise your initial time, run for 5 km, and then look again to your clock in order to find how much time did it take you to run this distance. If you find that it took you 22 minutes and 30 seconds, you will know that you are running 4 minutes 30 seconds/1 km or that you are running 16.2 seconds/meter (although your clock does not measure less than 1 second).  Best regards,  Iria

body: Dear Hunter27:  In the 2nd question, the post-condition has been expressed as an "equality" using only "=", because  the equalities in the preconditions or postconditions -in the method definition- can be expressed using "=" or "==".  In this case, "less than or greater than" were not used. The last case ("==") can be used "if" objects or variable are compared.    Regarding the 5th question, the "methods" annotated with annotations such as "@Before, @BeforeClass, @After or @AfterClass" are called "methods stubs" in Eclipse. It can be a manner to indicate that have a "life cycle" different from methods annotated with @Test. So, text fixtures are programmed in these kind of methods.  Regards,  Florina

body: Dear student:  The preconditions or postconditions are not Java statements. Whereas Java "assert" is a Java statement, thus, the equalities in the preconditions or postconditions -in the method definition- can be expressed using "=" or "==". The last case ("==") can be used "if" objects or variable are compared. Notice that "balance_prior" is not a Java variable defined inside the method, therefore, "==" cannot be used.  Regards,  Florina

title: Eclipse - loading the example projects - easy instructions
body:
I don't know if this will be helpful to anyone but this is the process I am following currently to load the sample projects into Eclipse on the MAC. For anyone still having problems importing this should be useful. .1. Locate the Eclipse projects folder that your projects are being saved to. *I chose to have them save to a folder on the desktop so it would be easier to find.*
![eclipse projects folder][1] .2. Unzip the downloaded file and copy the folder into the projects folder so that is alongside the other folders currently in use. .3. Right click on the "Package Explorer" inside of Eclipse and choose "Import"
![right click import project][2] .4. In the import Wizard expand "General" and select "Existing Projects into Workspace" and click Next>
![import wizard][3] .5. Click the browse button to select the folder of the project to import
![browse for project][4] .6. Select the folder you just copied in and click "Open"
![choose project folder for import][5] .7. Now that the directory appears click "Finish"
![finish importing project][6] .8. The new project will sit nicely next to the rest of your projects in the "Package Explorer"
![newly added project in eclipse][7]
.9. If you still need to add the JUnit library you can do so by right clicking on the project in the "Package Explorer" window and select properties.
![right click properties][8] .10. Select "Java Build Path" from the available properties. Click the "Libraries" (tab) and then click "Add Library"
![add junit][9] .11. Select JUnit and click Next>
![junit library][10] .12. Click Finish
![Junit 4][11] .13. Now that JUnit appears click "OK"
![junit added][12] .14. Looking in the "Package Explorer" window you should notice that the project will be loaded and will be able to use JUnit.

body: The index from where the inner loop starts increases in every iteration. Therefore, the running time is not quadratic in the strict mathematical sense.   If you we to find out the asymptotic runtime of an algorithm, we must take a look how the runtime scales:     Linear means: When we double the input size, the runtime doubles, too. Quadratic: When we double the input size, the runtime will  be squared.  Order-of-growth is a classification scheme, it discards leading coefficients.  We can make a doubling test and then calculate the ratio time(2N)/time(N) to get an intuition: size 6: 15 iterations size 12: 66 iterations → ratio: 4.4 size 24: 276 iterations → ratio: 11.5 size 48: 1128 iterations → ratio: 23.5 and so on (should really be made for larger values, 48 is still very small....)        If the order-of-growth was linear, the ratio would be the same.

body: You are absolutely right. A valuable test should contain testcases for every imaginable constellation (e.g.of inputs).     They should also contain inputs that are invalid/unexpected, not only for those that are valid/expected.    But: Even our best and most complete testcases can not *prove* the correctness of a program    There are two main goals to write a test:    1) Find the test cases where the program does not do what it is supposed to do. 2) Find the test cases where the program does what it is not supposed to do.  The tests that we are doing here in the course can only give us some introductory overview.    If you are interested in the subject: The following book is a classical (first edition 79) that I can highly recommend. I really love it, and I learned a lot from it:      G.F.Myers, T.Badgett, C.Sandler - The Art of Software Testing, 3rd edition (2011) You can read/download the [first chapter][1] here - it starts with an excellent  self assessment test ;)     [1]: http://media.wiley.com/product_data/excerpt/62/11180319/1118031962-54.pdf

A side effect is anything a method does besides computing and returning a value. possible side effects of methods:
   - change of instance or class field values
   - updating explicit parameters
   - any kind of output:
         · drawing something on the screen
         · writing to a file
         · sending data over a network connection


When we use any of these inside a conditional expression we get a « condition with side effects »
The following examples are meant to show these side effects. I leave it up to you to find more realistic examples.....

Example 1: the boolean method add(E e) has the side effect to add an element to a collection: List myList = new ArrayList(); System.out.println("myList before checking the condition: " + myList); // condition with side effect updates myList if (myList.add(5)) System.out.println("could add 5 to list"); System.out.println("myList after checking the condition: " + myList);

Example 2: assignment inside the condition: int myNumber = 0; System.out.println("myNumber before checking the condition: " + myNumber); // condition with side effect assignment if((myNumber=5) <10)System.out.println("Side effect: assigned 5 to a"); System.out.println("myNumber after checking the condition: " + myNumber);

Example 3: output
Lets say we defined the method canDivide as follows: public static boolean canDivide(int a, int b) { if (b == 0) { System.out.println("Can't divide by zero!"); return false; } System.out.println("This is a legal division"); return true; } // condition with side effect output if(canDivide(5, 10)) System.out.println("Side effect: additional output");

body: For a magic square of width n, the complexity of the checker is n^2, because it has to iterate through all the rows and columns.  I first wrote the individual checks for the whole checker, then I merged them into a single large loop with only two subloops, except the checking if all numbers are used.      public static boolean test(int[][] matrix, int dim){ 	 		// The sum of each diagonal, row and column should be 		int sum = dim * (dim * dim +1) / 2; 		 		// sums of diagonals 		int diag1 = 0; 		int diag2 = 0;  		//sum of current row and column 		int rowSum; 	    int colSum; 	     	    // array and counter used for checking if all numbers are used 	    int[] testArray = new int[dim*dim]; 	    int ctr = 0; 	     	    for (int i = 0; i < dim; i++) { 	    	diag1 += matrix[i][i]; 	    	rowSum = 0; 	    	colSum = 0; 	    	for (int j = 0; j < dim; j++) { 	    		rowSum += matrix[i][j]; 	    		colSum += matrix[j][i]; 	    		testArray[ctr] += matrix[i][j]; // while we're here, fill the testArray with all numbers 	    		ctr++; 	    	} 	    	if (rowSum != sum || colSum != sum ) {return false;} 	    	for (int j = dim-1; 0 <= j; j--) { 	    		if (i+j == dim -1) { 	    			diag2 += matrix[i][j]; 	    		} 	    	} 	    } 	    if (diag1 != sum || diag2 != sum ) {return false;} 	     	    // sort testArray, then check if the preceding number is by 1 smaller then the following  	    java.util.Arrays.sort(testArray); 	    for (int i = 1; i < testArray.length; i++) { 	    	if (testArray[i-1] != testArray[i] - 1 || testArray[i] > dim*dim) {return false;} 	    } 	 		return true;     }

To test a class, we write a new test class. In this test class, we define tests for *every* method in the class under test.
**To come up with a meaningful and useful test class, these test methods should aim to make fail the method we are testing**.
This means, we should choose test cases that (hopefully) find the circumstances under which the method *doesn't do* what it's *expected* to do - or under which the method *does* what it is *not expected* to do. I regret that the video only shows a fail caused by an error in the test itself!

Hello AndySpecht,
I'm a great fan of matrices - and so your solution caught my eye....
Like you, I had used a matrix to find a more robust and more general solution.
I scribbled it into my jotter - It looks like this: ![winMatrix][1] As you can see, it's a boolean matrix - except for the Ts (ties).
The next step was to transform the matrix into a boolean expression. The ties are already covered by the     `if (first_i == second_i) return TIE;`   
This is my boolean expression for the wins (all the 1s in the matrix): wins = first_i < second_i ? (first_i + second_i) % 2 == 1 : (first_i + second_i) % 2 == 0 ; return wins ? WIN : LOSE; This works for any length of the array (as long as each element beats the following) - even for unbalanced games (even length)
Further changes to the game only need to add (or delete) elements to the array. [1]: https://edxuploads.s3.amazonaws.com/14640353713444669.jpg

**This bridges the gap between pushing cohision to the max and avoiding code repetition!**

You could simplify it a little bit by using a boolean "row" instead of the char "rowCol" → one single if-else clause: if (row == true) { sumAux += matrix[row][col]; } else { sumAux += matrix[col][row]; } Another change that I would make is to call `testMagic()` from inside `testNormal` instead of repeating the same serie of method calls in both methods. There is one point that I consider as a bit questionable:
In `main()`, you only call `testMagic()` on the SagradaFamilia matrix (because you knew before that you will need it) - and not on the other matrices (because you already knew that both are normal magic squares).
Instead, you could for example write a method that tests any matrix whether it's a square matrix or normal square matrix and then pass the given matrices as input - and pretend knowing nothing about the outcomes ;)

body: package towersOfHanoi;  import java.util.*; /**  * Class that implements a solution to the Towers of Hanoi Problem   */ public class TowersOfHanoi {  	/** 	 * Prints solution to Tower of Hanoi Problem 	 *  	 * @param n  Number of disks, greater than zero 	 * @param source  Position of the disk to be moved, not null 	 * @param spare  Position used to hold discs, not null 	 * @return Number of moves taken to achieve solution. 	 */     public static int hanoiSolution(int n, String source, String spare, 	String destination) {     	int recursiveCount = 1;     	if (n<= 1) {     		System.out.println(source + " -> " + destination);     	} else {     		recursiveCount += hanoiSolution(n-1, source, destination, spare); 	    	System.out.println(source + " -> " + destination); 	    	recursiveCount += hanoiSolution(n-1, spare, source, destination);	     	}     	return recursiveCount;     }  	/** 	 * Accepts the number of disks in a Tower of Hanoi Problem, before printing 	 * the minimum number of moves to complete the problem and the number of 	 * moves taken to achieve the solution 	 */     public static void main(String[] args) { 	 	    Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in); 	    int discs; 	    int totalMoves; 	    String[] rods= {"A","B","C"}; 	    System.out.print("Please, enter the number of discs: "); 	    discs = scanner.nextInt(); 	    int  minMoves = (int) java.lang.Math.pow(2, discs)-1; 	    System.out.println("Minimum Number of Moves: "+minMoves);  	    /*A is the source of the discs, C their destination and B 	    the spare rod*/  	    //System.out.println("Solution: "); 	    totalMoves = hanoiSolution(discs, rods[0], rods[1], rods[2]); 	    System.out.println("Number of Steps: " + totalMoves); 	    scanner.close();     } }

body:
Although related to each other, cohesion and coupling are not antonyms! *Cohesion* represents the degree to which a part of a code base forms a logical unit.
High cohesion means keeping parts of code that are related to each other in a single place. *Coupling* represents the degree of interdependency of different units.
Low coupling is about separating unrelated parts of the code base as much as possible. **Code can have all four possible combinations of cohesion and coupling**: 1. **High cohesion and low coupling**
That's the ideal combination that we want to achive: Putting code that forms a logical unit into a single unit and minimizing the number of connections between two or more units. 2. **High cohesion and high coupling**
Example: A single piece of code that does all the work itself 3. **Low cohesion and high coupling**
This occurs when
a) the units are poorly chosen and don't form a logical unit and
b) unrelated parts are not separated 4. **Low cohision and low coupling**
Even parts of the code base that form a logical unit are separated. The code is over-decoupled in a way that the code looses its focus.

body: O(n^2) -  Does anyone have a more efficient solution?      public static boolean test(int[][] matrix, int dim) {     	// The sum of each diagonal, row and column should be     	int sum = dim * (dim * dim +1) / 2; 		 		boolean isMagicSquare = true;  		int sumDiag1 = 0, sumDiag2 = 0, sumSquare = 0, rowTotal;     	int[] colTotals = new int[dim];     	     	int i=0; int j;     	while ( i<dim && isMagicSquare) {     		j=0; rowTotal = 0;     		while (j<dim && isMagicSquare) {     			sumSquare += matrix[i][j];     			rowTotal += matrix[i][j];     			colTotals[j] += matrix[i][j];     			if (i==j) { sumDiag1 += matrix[i][j]; }     			if ((dim-1-i) == j) { sumDiag2 += matrix[i][j]; }     			     			if (j == dim - 1) { //check row     				isMagicSquare &= rowTotal == sum;     			}     			     			if (i == dim -1) { //check column     				isMagicSquare &= colTotals[j] == sum;     			}     			     			j++;     		}     		i++;     	}  		return isMagicSquare &&  				(dim * sum) == sumSquare && //check contains all numbers 				(sumDiag1 == sum) && //check primary diagonal  				(sumDiag2 == sum);   //check secondary diagonal     }

You cannot ignore the dimension of the matrix because the dim is in fact n. If you double n, the matrix will contain n² elements whether it's represented as a 2 dimensional martix or a 1 dimensional array. You can calculate the *empirical* order of growth as N raised to log₂(ratio T(2N)/T(N)) :
- dim: 3 → elements: 9 - dim: 6 → elements: 36 → ratio 36/9 == 4 - dim: 12 → elements: 144 → ratio 144/36 == 4 - etc. log₂(4) == 2 → order of growth is N² It's all about scaling: What happens if the problem size growth? Big Oh notation isn't an approximate model but used to develop an *upper bound* (to within a factor), a worst case scenario.
It gives us an idea about the problem size that can be solved in a certain (reasonable) amount of time. And we are interested in algorithms that can solve really huge problems. Therefore we need algorithms that scale well.

Hello TomTANGfromMacao, you cannot declare a method abstract that is already implemented.
That means, an abstract method declaration shouldn't contain any body. It should look like this: public abstract double calculatePerimeter(); When a class contains at least one abstract method, you must declare the class being abstract, too.
Every class that extends this abstract class must then provide an implementation for the abstract methods of its superclass. If not, the subclass must be declared abstract, too.
You cannot create instances of abstract classes themselves. In fact, when defining an abstract method, you are telling the compiler that all subclasses must provide an implementation (or declare themselves abstract). The sense of an abstract method is to tell the compiler that you want subclasses to provide this certain functionality. Different subclasses can than have different implementations of this abstract class.
In case of our example: All Figures will have a method called calculatePerimeter() that will return the perimeter of this shape.
How the perimeter will be calculated is defined in the concrete classes (Rectangle, Triangle, Circle, etc)
We don't need to know how each subclass implements this method, but we can be sure that each subclass has an implementation of this method. Any object of any of the subclasses will return the perimeter when we call the method on it: anyFigure.calculatePerimeter(); → returns the perimeter, whether anyFigure is a Rectangle, a Circle or a Triangle....

Concerning the main question:
First of all: Nothing is carved into the rock - So you might find different explanations.
Big O, big Omega, big Theta or Tilde notation are all about the complexity of algorithms. But big O is not a definitive answer. Commenly, these notations are used like this: - Tilde notation
→ provides the leading term (e.g. ~ 10 N²)
→ used to provide an approximtive model - Big Theta
→ provides the asymptotic order of growth (e.g. Θ(N<²))
→used to classify algorithms - Big Oh
→ provides Θ(N<²) and smaller (e.g. O(N²) ↔ **<=** N²)
→ used to develop upper bounds (worst case) - Big Omega
→ provides Θ(N<²) and larger (e.g. Ω(N²) ↔ **>=** N²)
→ used to develop lower bounds (best case) Don't hesitate to ask if you have more questions;)

That's a very interesting solution you came up with.
First of all: **Thumbs up for the consequent use of doc comments!!!** I hope you don't mind that I suggest some possible improvement. There is still some code repetition: Both, checkMagicSquare() and checkNormalMagicSquare() call the checkVectors() method - which has to do the most costly work...
If you change these methods such as the first checks a square matrix being magic and the latter checks a magic square being normal, you can avoid this code repetition: checkNormalMagicSquare() would only need to compare the magic constant against the normal magic constant and call checkNumbers().

The line « `test[element -1] = true;` » isn't part of the if clause. It will always be executed as long as the condition of the if clause doesn't evaluate to true. This would be clearer if the line wasn't indented! The variable "test" is a boolean array of length dim*dim. This means, you have an array that has as much elements as the matrix. On creation, all values are "false" by default. We want to check if the matrix contains all the numbers from 1 to dim*dim (including dim*dim)
The indices of the array cover the numbers 0 to dim*dim (exluding dim*dim)
By subtracting 1 from all numbers, the two ranges match exactly. When we iterate over the numbers in the matrix, we check the value of the array at index( number - 1):
→ if it is "false", we know that this number was not found before and we set the value to "true" (because: now, we found it)
→ if the value is "true", we know that we've seen this number before. We can stop and return "false" as the fact that the matrix contains non-unique elements implies that it can't contain all the numbers from 1 to dim*dim. (If one number appears twice, another *must* be missing) I hope this helps.

For many reasons (that to explain would lead too far), writing a secure encryption software yourself is very hard. And using a not really secure security might compromise all efforts. Luckily, we don't have to write the code ourselves: There exist many cryptographic APIs. The standard Sun [Java Cryptographic Architecture (JCA)][1] and [Java Cryptographic Extension (JCE)][2] are bundled in the JDK.
JCA is a framework for working with cryptography and part of the Java security API (java.security package).
JCE is a set of Java API's providing cryptographic services like encryption, secret Key Generation, Message Authentication code and Key Agreement (javax.crypto package).
The Open Web Application Security Project [OWASP][3] is a good starting point for all security questions you may have. It offers also a guide [how to use the JCE][4] (and lots of code snippets). For a more lightwight API, you might want to explore [Bouncycastle][5] [1]: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/crypto/CryptoSpec.html [2]: http://www.oracle.com/technetwork/java/javase/downloads/jce-7-download-432124.html [3]: https://www.owasp.org/index.php/Main_Page [4]: https://www.owasp.org/index.php/Using_the_Java_Cryptographic_Extensions [5]: http://www.bouncycastle.org/java.html

body:
To understand the difference between cohision and coupling, it helps to look at the "scope" they refer to: **Cohision** looks **inside a module**, at the parts that form the module (e.g. a method or a class) and asks: How strong belong the different parts together? Do they *focus on the same task*?
High cohesion means that the parts of this module *belong together* in the sense that they work on a same task. **Coupling** looks **between different modules** and asks: How much depend these different modules from each other? If I apply changes to one of them, do I have to change the other? (We talk also of coupling when a global variable is changed etc.)
High coupling means that modules strongly depend on each other. This doesn't mean that they belong together, but that they "infuence" each other. In **OOP**, we want to achieve **high cohesion** (classes and methods that concentrate on one single task). At the same time, we want to keep the **coupling low** (no interdependency between classes and methods - if we have to change something in the code, we can do so at one single place).

title: Rule of Thumb ?
body: This is a great list of ethical dilemma's.   I have been involved with several different ethical discussions in the past related to software development and several were addressed or 'eased' by putting general 'rule of thumb' behaviors in place which provided a limitation on what to address or to prioritize.  Understanding different aspects of what was needed now, 3 months from now, 6 months from now.  For example for **Ethical dilemma No. 12: How much should future consequences influence present decisions**.  The software development team came to an agreement which limited the scope i.e. they would only look at or evaluate the risk of future consequences which might occur within the next  6 months.  Or as another example for **Ethical dilemma No. 10. How much monitoring is really warranted**, the scope of this question was limited by agreeing to a general rule of thumb that the immediate programming needs would only solve for certain questions which were being asked by stakeholders and/or used to promote a future capability or minimize an immediate risk. I am wondering if anyone else has also been involved with similar discussions and how they were approached?

body:
In code design, there are always some tradeoffs that we have to handle. At the end, it's the programmer who decides...
The overall goal is to write code that is not only correct, but also to write code that is easily maintainable, by the programmer and other programmers. Therefore we have the two additional goals: Maximize maintainability and maximize readability. And I would add a third one, reusability. The checkNormalMagicSquare() would not be dependent on the implementation of checkMagicSquare. No matter what is the actual implementation of checkMagicSquare, checkNormalMagicSquare just calls the method and gets the result. This will still work if we apply changes to the checkMagicSquare method.
And that's exactly what we want to achieve: The independence of the actual implementation. The problem I see in your main method is not the call to different methods as such. Of course we (or any user of the program) might want to do different checks.
What I want to point to is the fact that *you call different methods to get the required output because you already know which magic square is normal and which is not*.
To see what I mean, you might want to change the names (only the names) of magicSquareJupiter and magicSquareSagradaFamilia and then decide if the result still matches what we wanted to achieve in this exercise. Please take my posts here not as a devaluation of your work - it's more the opposite.
When I stumbled over your code, I saw that your solution implements a lot of the principles we talked about in this course - in some parts very consequently, in others a bit less.
It's obvious that you reasoned a lot about the design, what should be done where etc. - so, take my posts as "fuel" for further reasoning ;)

title: Ethical Dilemmas
body: Ethical dilemma No. 1: Log files -- what to save and how to handle them Whenever I am generating logs or analytics, I push everything through a function that requires data sensitivity be passed as a parameter. Sensitive data is only sent to secure services and private data is stripped unless the application is being run within a lab environment.  Ethical dilemma No. 2: Whether -- and how -- to transform users into products People often criticize these models, but the truth is that many of the services we use today wouldn't be here without them.  Ethical dilemma No. 3: How free does content really want to be? This is a major problem for SEO. On one hand you want certain content to be redistributed with a backlink while on the other hand you don't want your content to be scraped for spam content on ad farms etc. Rel canonical is a partial solution, but it is up to the scraper to respect it.  Ethical dilemma No. 4: How much protection is enough A base-line should be developed based on both business and security considerations - this baseline should be applied across the board except where applicable laws require a higher level of security.  Ethical dilemma No. 5: To bug-fix or not to bug-fix? Relevant links: https://wiki.gnome.org/Bugsquad/TriageGuide#StepsOfTriaging http://blog.smartbear.com/quality/responsible-bug-reporting-and-triage/  Of course, business considerations must also be factored in, but never in a way that would ignore critical bugs or bugs that impact security.  Ethical dilemma No. 6: How much to code -- or compromise -- to prevent misuse This depends greatly on the project and involved business interests. I don't have a generalized answer.  Ethical dilemma No. 7: How far to defend customers against data requests This depends on the purpose of the application and the mission of the developer/business creating it. me too, I regret edX's decision to not offer honor code certificates any more - and there are many others who do so.
You might want to read the [edX blog][1] about their new policy.
There is a financial assistance program for those who can't afford to pay the fee.
This means: You have to deliver even more personal data to get 90% off But I must recognize: At least, all content is accessible for all learners, including all quizzes, assignments and exams.
